Listing 18.1: Production Agent Harness – Core Implementation

Key Design Decisions in the Implementation
• Context enforcement happens on every add_message call, not just before LLM calls.
This prevents silent overflow.
• Parallel tool execution via asyncio.gather reduces latency when the model requests
multiple tools simultaneously.
• Loop detection uses content hashing over a sliding window, catching both exact repeats
and near-repeats.
• Approval gates are per-tool, not per-run, allowing fine-grained control over which actions
require human sign-off.
• Structured logging with a run_id makes it easy to trace a single agent run across
distributed logs.
• Exponential backoff is applied at the tool level, not the LLM level, since tool failures are
more common and more recoverable.
How Do You Test an Agent Harness?
Testing agents is fundamentally different from testing deterministic software. Key strategies: (1)
Unit test each component (context manager, tool executor, loop detector) in isolation with
mocked dependencies. (2) Integration test the full harness against a mock LLM that returns
scripted responses. (3) Evaluation harness: run the agent on a benchmark of tasks with known
correct answers and measure success rate. (4) Adversarial testing: deliberately inject malformed
tool outputs and verify graceful failure. (5) Regression testing: replay past production traces
and verify that outputs do not regress after changes.

Summary
The agent harness is the engineering foundation that transforms a language model into a capable,
reliable agent. The key takeaways from this section are:
• Context is a finite, precious resource. Enforce budgets explicitly, count tokens with the
model’s exact tokenizer, and compress history proactively.
414

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

• Prompts are code. Version-control them, test them, and assemble them modularly from
components.
• Tools are the agent’s actuators. Define them precisely, sandbox their execution, and handle
their outputs defensively.
• Orchestration patterns are not one-size-fits-all. ReAct for exploratory tasks, Plan-andExecute for structured tasks, multi-agent for complex decomposable tasks.
• State management is a first-class concern. Design state schemas upfront; retrofitting
them is painful.
• Errors are inevitable; graceful recovery is a feature. Implement retry logic, loop
detection, and informative failure messages.
• Observability is not optional. You cannot debug what you cannot see. Instrument
everything from day one.
• Production concerns compound. Latency, cost, rate limits, and evaluation all interact.
Address them systematically, not as afterthoughts.
Harness Distillation: Baking Scaffolding into Weights
The harness engineering techniques in this chapter raise a natural question: can the behavioral
gains of a specialized harness be trained into the model weights, so the harness can be removed
at deployment? This is the goal of harness distillation, covered in Section 12.6 (LLM Agentic
Training). The Harness-Zero approach shows that a model trained under a specialized harness h∗
and then deployed under only a generic harness h can exceed the performance of the base model
with h∗ still attached — recovering over 80% of harness-exclusive behaviors while eliminating the
runtime scaffolding overhead.

Chapter 19

Loop Engineering
The simplest agentic pattern is a loop: generate, observe, act, repeat. But production agents require
more than a while loop — they need principled context management, adaptive orchestration that
responds to intermediate results, mechanisms for detecting and escaping stagnation, and the ability
to escalate to human oversight when confidence falls below a threshold. This chapter covers loop
engineering as a discipline: the five loop primitives, context engineering as the layer beneath the
loop, parallel subagent fleet execution, and cognitive escalation with uncertainty-driven handoff.
GAS Connection — Loop Engineering
The GAS Monitor agent is a production ReAct loop, and the GAS pipeline as a whole is a multiagent loop. The following chapter’s patterns for loop design, termination, and failure handling are
directly implemented in capstone_gas/gas_system.py.
Anatomy of a production loop (§ Anatomy of a Production Loop). The Monitor’s
loop in monitor_node() has four phases: (1) Observe: read the latest CGM reading from
state["current_reading"]; (2) Reason: compute the alert level using the chain-of-thought
prompt (“current glucose is X mg/dL; trend is Y; this is/is not anomalous because...”); (3) Act:
write the alert level to GASState; (4) Route: the Supervisor checks if the alert level exceeds the
escalation threshold and routes to the Advisor if so.
Loop patterns (§ Loop Patterns). The GAS uses two loop patterns: (1) ReAct for the
Monitor (reason then act); (2) Reflection for the Safety Critic (generate a verdict, then check it
against constitutional rules in safety_node()).
Termination engineering (§ Termination Engineering). The GAS implements two termination conditions: (1) Threshold: alert_level in ("high", "critical") → escalate to Advisor;
(2) Retry budget: maximum 2 Advisor–Safety Critic cycles (tracked by state["iteration"] in
GASState) before the Supervisor routes to END and flags the case for human review.
Failure modes (§ Failure Modes and Anti-Patterns). The GAS has one known loop
failure mode: the Advisor–Safety Critic cycle can repeat if the Advisor consistently generates
recommendations with safety_score < 0.7. This is prevented by the iteration counter in
GASState: after 2 retries, the Supervisor routes to END rather than cycling indefinitely.
Context management in long-running loops (§ Context Management in Long-Running
Loops). The GAS pipeline runs continuously for the duration of a patient’s monitoring session.
The readings_history field in GASState accumulates CGM readings; the GASLLMClient enforces
a fixed context window to prevent overflow while preserving the most recent patient history.
The evolution of how practitioners interact with LLM-based agents has followed a remarkably
consistent trajectory. In 2022–2024, the primary skill was prompt engineering: crafting the right
words to elicit the desired response from a single model call. By 2025, the focus shifted to context
engineering—curating the full set of tokens the model sees at inference time, including retrieved
documents, tool outputs, and conversation history [11]. In the previous chapter we covered harness
engineering: designing the runtime environment—tools, sandboxes, memory, and guardrails—that
surrounds an agent. Loop engineering [295] is the next layer in this progression: designing the
iterative control structure that drives an agent toward a goal autonomously, without requiring a
human to type the next instruction at each turn.
416

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

From Prompt to Loop: The Engineering Progression
1. Prompt engineering: Optimize what you say to the model (2022–2024)
2. Context engineering: Optimize everything the model sees (2025)
3. Harness engineering: Optimize the environment the agent runs in (2025–2026)
4. Loop engineering: Optimize the cycle that keeps the agent working toward a goal (2026)
Each layer wraps the previous one without replacing it. You still write prompts; you still curate
context; you still build a harness. Loop engineering puts all of it in motion.
The phrase was coined in June 2026 after Peter Steinberger [357] argued that developers should
stop prompting coding agents directly and instead design systems that prompt those agents—a
sentiment validated by Boris Cherny, who leads Claude Code at Anthropic, noting that his role had
shifted entirely to writing the external execution loops that coordinate model actions [54]. This is
not merely a tooling preference. It reflects a structural reality: when a single agent run may last an
hour and modify dozens of files, the highest-leverage engineering is no longer in the prompt—it is in
the loop that keeps the agent productive, verified, and on-goal throughout.

19.1

Context Engineering: The Layer Beneath the Loop

Before a loop can run, something must decide what the model sees at each step. That discipline is
context engineering: the formal practice of curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens in
the context window during inference. It is the layer beneath the loop—the mechanism by which the
loop’s state is translated into model input.
The term was popularized by Tobi Lütke (CEO of Shopify) in June 2025 [257], who described it as
the emerging core skill for working with AI agents. Anthropic formalized the definition in September
2025 as “curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens during inference.” Andrej Karpathy
endorsed the framing, describing it as “the delicate art and science of filling the context window with
just the right information for the next step” [188]. The convergence of these definitions reflects a
practical reality: as context windows grew from 4K to 128K to 1M tokens, the question of what to
put in them became as important as the question of what to ask.
Context engineering is not prompt engineering. Prompt engineering optimizes the instruction—the
words that direct the model’s behavior. Context engineering optimizes the information environment—
the full set of documents, tool outputs, history, and state that the model reasons over. In a single-turn
interaction, the distinction is minor. In a multi-step agent loop, it is the difference between a model
that has the information it needs to act correctly and one that is flying blind.
Key techniques.

Context engineering draws on several complementary methods:

• Dynamic context assembly: Selecting and composing context from multiple sources (retrieved documents, tool outputs, memory stores) at each loop iteration rather than using a
fixed template.
• RAG integration: Retrieving task-relevant documents or code snippets and injecting them
into the context window, replacing stale or generic background knowledge with precise, current
information.
• Tool-output summarization: Compressing verbose tool outputs (e.g., long file listings, test
runner logs) before inserting them into context, preserving signal while conserving token budget.
• Conversation history management: Deciding which prior turns to retain verbatim, which
to summarize, and which to drop entirely—a rolling compression problem that becomes critical
in long agent runs.
417

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

• Token budget allocation: Explicitly partitioning the context window across competing
information sources to ensure the model always has room to generate a useful response.
Context Window Budget Allocation (Typical Agent Loop)
Component

Budget

Notes

System prompt
Retrieved documents / RAG
Conversation / action history
Generation budget

10–15%
20–30%
30–40%
20–30%

Stable; defines agent role, tools, constraints
Dynamic; refreshed each iteration
Compressed as run lengthens
Reserved for model output; never compress below this

These are guidelines, not hard rules. Long-horizon coding agents may allocate more to history; single-step
QA agents may allocate more to retrieved documents. The key invariant: always reserve the generation
budget before filling the rest.

Context engineering within a loop. In a loop, context engineering operates at every iteration.
At each step t, the loop controller must decide: which prior observations o<t to retain, which to
summarize, which retrieved documents are still relevant, and how to compose the new context st
from these components. This is not a one-time design decision—it is a dynamic policy that runs
alongside the agent policy πθ . A poorly designed context policy causes the model to lose track of its
goal, repeat actions it has already taken, or fail to use information it retrieved two steps earlier. A
well-designed one keeps the model’s “working memory” aligned with the current state of the task
throughout the entire run.
Context Engineering vs. Loop Engineering
Context engineering answers: what does the model see at step t? Loop engineering answers: what
happens after the model acts at step t? They are complementary. The loop determines the sequence
of actions and observations; context engineering determines how those observations are represented
when the model takes its next action. You cannot do loop engineering well without doing context
engineering well—the loop’s state is only useful if it is correctly encoded in the model’s context.

19.2

Loop Engineering as Inference-Time Reinforcement Learning

The central insight that makes loop engineering relevant to this book is that a well-engineered agent
loop is structurally identical to an RL optimization process operating at inference time—without
gradient updates to the model weights:
st = context(st−1 , at−1 , ot−1 )

(state = accumulated context)

at = πθ (st )

(action = model generation)

ot = env(at )

(observation = tool/environment feedback)

rt = verify(st , at , ot )

(reward = verification signal)

(19.1)

The loop continues until rt exceeds a success threshold or a termination condition triggers. The
“policy” πθ is not updated via gradients; instead, the state is updated—observations, error messages,
and reflections are appended to the context, conditioning the same frozen model to produce better
actions on subsequent iterations. This is precisely the mechanism behind Reflexion [344]: the model
improves across iterations not by learning new weights but by reading its own failure history.
The Loop–RL Correspondence
Consider the standard RL objective maxπ E[

PT

t
t=0 γ rt ]. In loop engineering:

• Policy π: The frozen LLM, conditioned on accumulating context
• State st : The context window contents at step t
• Action at : The model’s generated output (code edit, tool call, message)
418

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

• Environment: The tools, filesystem, test runner, linter—anything that produces observations
• Reward rt : The verification signal (tests pass, linter clean, metric improves)
• Discount γ: Implicit in the loop’s budget—later steps are costlier and less likely to succeed
• Episode: One complete loop execution from goal specification to termination
The critical difference from training-time RL: the policy weights are frozen. “Learning” happens
purely through state accumulation—the model receives richer conditioning as the loop progresses.
This is analogous to in-context learning, but with the environment actively shaping what the
model sees.
This correspondence is not merely metaphorical. It has direct engineering consequences:
1. Reward design matters: Just as in RLHF, a poorly specified reward (verification criterion)
leads to reward hacking—the agent satisfying the letter of the check while violating its intent
(e.g., deleting a failing test to turn CI green).
2. Exploration–exploitation trade-off : A loop that repeats the same failing approach exhibits
poor exploration. Mechanisms like Reflexion [344] add explicit exploration via self-critique,
analogous to entropy bonuses in PPO.
3. Horizon and discount: Longer loops face compounding errors and context degradation, just
as long-horizon RL suffers from credit assignment difficulty. Budget caps serve as effective
horizons.
4. State representation: Context management (compaction, pruning, externalization) is the
loop-engineering equivalent of state representation design in RL—both determine whether the
agent can reason effectively about its situation.

19.3

Anatomy of a Production Loop

A functional loop requires five structural primitives [295] plus external state persistence:

19.3.1

The Five Primitives
Table 19.1: The five structural primitives of loop engineering.

Primitive

Role in the Loop

RL Analogue

Automations

Trigger the loop on schedule or event

Automations. Automations are the heartbeat that transforms a single agent run into a true loop.
They define when and why a loop fires—on a cron schedule, in response to a webhook, or triggered by
a file-system event. Without automations, you have an agent; with them, you have a self-sustaining
system. Production examples include nightly CI failure triage, hourly dependency-vulnerability scans,
and post-commit review passes.
419

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

Worktrees (Isolation). The moment multiple agents run in parallel, file-level conflicts become
the dominant failure mode. Git worktrees—separate working directories sharing repository history—
provide isolation: each agent operates on its own branch without the possibility of write conflicts
with siblings. This is the same principle as running independent rollout workers in distributed RL
(Section 11.2): parallelism requires isolation.
Skills. Skills (Chapter 24) encode project knowledge that the agent would otherwise re-derive from
scratch every cycle. In the loop context, skills serve as persistent conditioning—the conventions,
build procedures, and constraints that remain stable across iterations. Without skills, each loop
iteration begins cold; with them, the agent compounds knowledge across runs without exhausting
the context window on rediscovered facts.
Connectors. Connectors—typically implemented via MCP (Chapter 23)—extend the loop’s action
space beyond the filesystem. A loop that can only read and write files is limited; one connected to
the issue tracker, CI system, staging environment, and team communication channel can close the
full feedback loop: detect problem → fix → validate → deploy → notify.
Sub-agents (Maker–Checker Separation). The most critical structural principle in loop
engineering is separating the agent that produces output from the agent that evaluates it. A model
grading its own output is analogous to a student marking their own exam—the incentives are
misaligned. A dedicated verification sub-agent, potentially running a different model or at higher
reasoning effort, provides the independent evaluation that makes unattended operation trustworthy.
This mirrors the actor–critic architecture in RL: the actor (generator) proposes actions; the critic
(verifier) evaluates them.

19.3.2

External State: The Loop’s Memory

Every primitive above operates within a single iteration. External state is what connects iterations
across time. Because LLMs are stateless between invocations—the model forgets everything not in
its current context—the loop’s continuity must live on disk: a markdown progress file, a structured
database, or a version-controlled log. This external state serves three functions:
1. Progress tracking: What has been attempted, what succeeded, what remains.
2. Failure memory: Which approaches were tried and failed, preventing the loop from oscillating
between identical dead ends.
3. Handoff context: When the loop escalates to a human or a subsequent run, the state file
provides a complete audit trail.
State Is Not Optional
A loop without external state is a loop with amnesia. It will re-attempt failed approaches, lose
track of partial progress, and provide no audit trail when things go wrong. The state mechanism
need not be complex—a markdown file committed to git after each iteration is often sufficient—but
it must exist.

19.4

The Loop in Pseudocode

Stripped to its essence, every agent loop is a control structure closer to a thermostat or a REPL
than to a conversation:
def agent_loop ( goal : str , max_steps : int = 50 , budget : TokenBudget = None ) :
" " " The canonical agent loop structure . " " "
state = initialize_state ( goal )
# Load external state + goal

420

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

for step in range ( max_steps ) :
# 1. Reason about current state ( ReAct - style )
thought = model . reason ( state )
# 2. Choose and execute action
action = model . choose_action ( state )
observation = environment . execute ( action )
# 3. Update state with new information
state = update_state ( state , thought , action , observation )
# 4. Compact context if approaching window limit
if state . token_count > CONTEXT_BUDGET * 0.8:
state = compact ( state )
# Summarize old steps
# 5. Check termination conditions
if verifier . passes ( state , goal ) : # Deterministic check
persist_state ( state , status = " success " )
return Success ( state )
if no_progress_detected ( state , window =3) :
persist_state ( state , status = " stuck " )
return escalate_to_human ( state )
if budget and budget . exhausted () :
persist_state ( state , status = " budget_exceeded " )
return escalate_to_human ( state )
# Hard cap reached
persist_state ( state , status = " max_steps " )
return escalate_to_human ( state )

Everything interesting in loop engineering is a decision about one of these lines: what constitutes
a valid goal, how verifier.passes is implemented, how compact preserves relevant history while
discarding noise, and how no_progress_detected avoids both premature termination and infinite
cycling.

19.5

Loop Patterns

Building on the agent design patterns introduced in Chapter 21, loop engineering recognizes a
hierarchy of increasingly autonomous patterns:

19.5.1

The Validation Loop

The simplest and most common pattern: generate, validate against a deterministic check, retry on
failure.
Validation Loop: Fix Until Tests Pass
failure_log = []
for attempt in range ( MAX_ATTEMPTS ) :
result = run_tests ()
if result . passed :
break # Success -- exit loop
fix = model . generate (
f " Fix this test failure :\ n { result . errors }\ n "
f " Previous attempts that failed : { failure_log } "
)
apply_patch ( fix )
failure_log . append ( result . errors )

Termination: Tests pass (success) or retry budget exhausted (escalate).
421

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

Key property: The verification signal is deterministic—the test runner produces an objective
pass/fail that the model cannot argue around.
This pattern succeeds because its reward signal is crisp. The test runner serves as an incorruptible
critic—unlike LLM-as-judge evaluation, it cannot be persuaded or fooled.

19.5.2

The Reflexion Loop

Extends the validation loop with explicit self-critique between attempts [344]. After each failure, the
agent writes a natural-language reflection (“I failed because I modified the wrong function—the error
traces back to the import, not the implementation”) into an episodic memory buffer. Subsequent
attempts read this buffer, enabling learning within an episode without weight updates.
Reflexion: In-Context Learning from Failure
The Reflexion loop adds three components beyond basic retry:
1. Actor: Executes the task
2. Evaluator: Provides the reward signal (tests, metrics, or LLM judge)
3. Self-Reflection: Writes a verbal “lesson learned” to episodic memory
The reflection memory persists across attempts, giving the agent a mechanism to avoid repeating
identical failures. Empirically, Reflexion achieves 91% pass@1 on HumanEval (vs. 67% baseline),
demonstrating that verbal self-critique can substitute for weight updates in iterative settings [344].

19.5.3

The Evaluator-Optimizer Loop

A two-model architecture [11, 259]: one model generates a candidate, a separate model evaluates it
against explicit criteria and returns structured feedback. The generator incorporates this feedback
and produces an improved version. The cycle repeats until the evaluator’s score exceeds a threshold
or the iteration budget is consumed.
The critical design choice is whether the evaluator is deterministic (compiler, test suite, linter)
or probabilistic (another LLM). Deterministic evaluators produce reliable convergence; probabilistic
evaluators are necessary for subjective criteria but introduce the risk of evaluator–generator collusion.

19.5.4

The Hierarchical Loop

A meta-loop spawns and monitors sub-loops. An orchestrator agent decomposes a high-level goal
into subtasks, assigns each to a specialized sub-agent running its own loop, monitors their progress,
and synthesizes results. This mirrors hierarchical RL [23]: a high-level policy selects sub-goals while
low-level policies execute them.
Hierarchical Loop: Overnight Repository Maintenance
# Outer loop : runs nightly via automation
for issue in triage_agent . i d e n t i f y _ a c t i o n a b l e _ i s s u e s () :
# Inner loop : one sub - agent per issue , isolated worktree

goal = issue . description ,

)

The outer loop (triage) operates on a schedule. Inner loops (fixes) are ephemeral and task-scoped.
The review agent provides the maker–checker separation. State is persisted across nightly runs.

19.5.5

The Autonomous Research Loop

Karpathy’s AutoResearch [189] demonstrates a tightly constrained research loop: the agent modifies
a training script, runs a time-bounded experiment (e.g., 5 minutes on a GPU), reads the validation
metric, and decides whether to commit the change (metric improved) or roll back (metric degraded).
The loop continues indefinitely, exploring the hyperparameter and architectural space through
iterative experimentation.
This pattern works because the reward signal is scalar and unambiguous: validation loss either
decreased or it did not. The tight time bound per iteration prevents any single failed experiment
from consuming excessive resources.

19.6

Verification Engineering

Verification is the reward function of loop engineering. Its quality determines whether the loop
converges to the correct answer, converges to a wrong one, or fails to converge at all. This section
establishes a hierarchy of verification strategies ordered by reliability.

19.6.1

The Verification Hierarchy
Table 19.2: Verification strategies ordered by reliability.

The Verification Principle
A loop is only as trustworthy as its least reliable verification step. Wherever a deterministic check
exists, use it. Reserve LLM-as-judge for criteria that genuinely cannot be mechanically verified.
Never let the generating model judge its own output—the maker and the checker must be separate.

19.6.2

Deterministic vs. Probabilistic Verification

Deterministic verifiers (compilers, test suites, linters) are the gold standard because they produce an
objective pass/fail that the model cannot game through persuasion. A test either passes or it does
not—no amount of eloquent reasoning changes the verdict.
Probabilistic verifiers (LLM-as-judge) are necessary for tasks without mechanical checks—code
quality, documentation clarity, UX improvement—but they introduce failure modes:
423

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

• Self-evaluation bias: If the same model generates and evaluates, it will be lenient with its
own output.
• Evaluator gaming: Over many iterations, the generator may learn to produce outputs that
satisfy the evaluator’s surface patterns without achieving genuine quality.
• Evaluator inconsistency: The same LLM-judge may score identical outputs differently across
runs due to sampling variance.
Mitigation strategies include using a different (often stronger) model as evaluator, providing
explicit rubrics with binary criteria, and periodically calibrating the LLM-judge against human
judgments.

19.7

Termination Engineering

The signature failure of a naive loop is that it never stops. Termination design is not an afterthought—
it is half the engineering.

19.7.1

Termination Conditions

A production loop carries multiple independent exit conditions:
1. Goal achieved: The verifier confirms the objective is met. This is the only successful
termination.
2. Hard iteration cap: Maximum number of loop steps (typically 20–50). Prevents unbounded
execution regardless of other conditions.
3. Budget exhaustion: Token count, wall-clock time, or monetary cost exceeds a predefined
limit.
4. No-progress detection: The last k iterations produced no measurable change in state—the
loop is oscillating or stuck. This is the most important safety mechanism after the hard cap.
5. Fatal error: An unrecoverable condition (missing credentials, infrastructure failure) that no
amount of iteration can resolve.
No-Progress Detection: The Stagnation Circuit Breaker
Detecting stagnation requires tracking a progress signal across iterations. Common approaches:
• Output hash comparison: If the last 3 agent outputs or file states are identical, the loop
is cycling.
• Error repetition: The same error message appears in k consecutive iterations.
• Metric plateau: A numerical signal (test pass rate, validation loss) has not improved by ϵ
in k steps.
• Diff entropy: The size of code changes per iteration is decreasing toward zero—the agent
is making progressively smaller, inconsequential edits.
When stagnation is detected, the correct action is escalation, not continued iteration. The loop
saves its state and hands control to a human or a higher-level orchestrator.
424

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

19.7.2

The Exploration Problem

A loop stuck in a local minimum—repeating the same failing approach with minor variations—is
exhibiting the exploration–exploitation failure familiar from RL. Mechanisms to promote exploration
within loops:
• Reflection-based exploration: After k failed attempts, trigger a reflection step that explicitly asks the model to consider fundamentally different approaches (analogous to entropy
regularization in PPO [337]).
• Temperature escalation: Increase sampling temperature after consecutive failures to encourage diverse outputs.
• Strategy memory: Record not just failed actions but failed strategies. “Approach A (modify
the handler) failed 3 times; try approach B (rewrite the schema) instead.”
• Fresh sub-agent: Spawn a new sub-agent with a clean context window—it cannot fall into
the rut that the accumulated context may have created.

19.8

Cognitive Escalation and Uncertainty-Driven Handoff

The escalator is named as one of the five loop primitives (Section 19.7), but its design is rarely specified
in detail. The standard treatment—“when stagnation is detected, hand off to a human”—conflates
three distinct failure modes that require different responses:
1. Stagnation: the agent is making no progress (output hash unchanged, metric plateau). The
loop is stuck but the task may be solvable with a different approach.
2. Epistemic uncertainty: the agent is making progress but is uncertain whether its current
trajectory is correct. It has not failed yet, but it recognizes that it may be operating on flawed
assumptions.
3. Capability boundary: the task requires a capability the agent does not have. No amount of
iteration will produce a correct result.
Each failure mode calls for a different escalation response. Stagnation calls for strategy diversification or human guidance on approach. Epistemic uncertainty calls for a confidence checkpoint—a
structured pause to verify assumptions before proceeding. A capability boundary calls for immediate
escalation with a clear statement of what is missing.

19.8.1

Confidence Estimation Mid-Task

A production loop should maintain a running estimate of its own confidence in the current trajectory.
This is not a single number but a structured signal with several components:
Verifier confidence. If the loop uses a verifier (a secondary model or rule-based checker that
evaluates each step), the verifier’s output score is the most direct confidence signal. A verifier
score that has been declining over the last k steps is a strong indicator of trajectory degradation.
Assumption stability. Track the key assumptions the agent made at the start of the task (e.g.,
“the API endpoint is at /v2/users”). If tool outputs contradict these assumptions, confidence
should drop sharply.
Budget consumption rate. If the agent has consumed 80% of its token budget but completed
only 30% of the task, the probability of successful completion within budget is low. This is a
quantifiable signal.
425

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

Novelty detection. If the current situation is far from any situation in the agent’s training distribution or past experience (measured by embedding distance from the nearest retrieved memory),
the agent should treat its own outputs with lower confidence.

19.8.2

Dynamic Escalation Thresholds

Static escalation thresholds (“escalate after 20 iterations”) are brittle. A task that requires 50
iterations to complete correctly will be escalated prematurely; a task that should complete in 5
iterations but is stuck will not be escalated until iteration 20. Dynamic thresholds adapt to the task:
Budget-proportional thresholds. Express escalation conditions as fractions of the allocated
budget rather than absolute counts. “Escalate if verifier score has not improved in the last 20% of
the iteration budget” scales correctly across tasks of different lengths.
Bayesian confidence tracking. Maintain a posterior over task success probability, updated at
each iteration. Escalate when the posterior falls below a threshold pmin :
P (success | history1:t ) < pmin =⇒ escalate.
The prior can be set from historical success rates on similar tasks; the likelihood update uses the
verifier score at each step.
Asymmetric costs. In high-stakes domains (healthcare, finance, legal), the cost of a false negative
(proceeding when the agent should have escalated) is much higher than the cost of a false positive
(escalating unnecessarily). Set pmin accordingly: a medical agent should escalate at pmin = 0.9; a
content summarization agent can tolerate pmin = 0.5.

19.8.3

Escalation Handoff Protocol

When the escalation condition fires, the quality of the handoff determines whether the human or
higher-level orchestrator can efficiently resolve the situation. A minimal escalation handoff package
contains:
1. Task statement: the original goal, verbatim.
2. Progress summary: what has been accomplished, what has been attempted and failed, and
what the current state is.
3. Escalation reason: which condition fired (stagnation, epistemic uncertainty, capability boundary) and the supporting evidence (verifier scores, assumption violations, budget consumption).
4. Resumption context: the full loop state, serialized so that execution can resume from the
current point after the human provides guidance—without restarting from scratch.
426

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

5. Suggested next steps: the agent’s best guess at what the human should do, clearly labeled
as a suggestion, not a decision.
Escalation Handoff in the Guardian Angel System
The GAS Safety Critic implements a structured escalation path. When the Safety Critic’s
confidence in a glucose management recommendation falls below a threshold (currently 0.7 on a
0–1 scale), it does not silently pass or fail the recommendation—it generates a structured escalation
message to the caregiver node containing: the original recommendation, the specific safety concern,
the confidence score, and a suggested conservative alternative. The caregiver node then decides
whether to act on the original recommendation, the alternative, or escalate to a human clinician.
This three-level escalation (agent → caregiver agent → human) is the production pattern for
high-stakes agentic systems.
Escalation Is Not Failure
A well-designed escalation is a success: the agent correctly recognized the limits of its own
competence and handed off before causing harm. The failure mode is an agent that proceeds
confidently past its competence boundary. Design escalation as a first-class capability, not a
fallback of last resort. Measure escalation rate as a quality metric: too low means the agent is
overconfident; too high means the task decomposition or capability scoping is wrong.

19.9

Failure Modes and Anti-Patterns

19.9.1

The Loopmaxxing Trap

“Loopmaxxing”—the assumption that running an agent through enough iterations will eventually
produce a correct solution—is the loop-engineering equivalent of believing that enough compute
solves all problems. It fails for the same reason that pure random search fails: without a gradient
signal pointing toward improvement, iteration alone is not optimization.
Loopmaxxing manifests when:
• The goal lacks a checkable success condition (“improve the user experience”)
• The verification signal is too coarse (binary pass/fail on a 1000-test suite provides no gradient
toward the fix)
• The agent lacks the capability to solve the problem regardless of iteration count
The antidote is recognizing that loops amplify engineering capability—they do not replace it. A
loop with a poorly specified objective will pursue the wrong thing with great efficiency.

19.9.2

Comprehension Debt

When a loop modifies code faster than the engineering team can review it, the gap between what
exists in the repository and what humans understand grows—comprehension debt [295]. Unlike
technical debt (which the code carries), comprehension debt lives in the team’s heads. It compounds
silently until a crisis forces someone to debug code whose design decisions, structural dependencies,
and edge cases are entirely unmapped.
Loops Amplify Both Productivity and Risk
A well-designed loop accelerates work the engineer understands deeply. A loop used to avoid
understanding the work creates an accelerating spiral of incomprehension. Same mechanism,
opposite outcomes. The difference is whether the human stays the engineer or becomes merely the
person who presses “go.”
427

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

19.9.3

Reward Hacking in Loops

Just as RL agents exploit reward misspecification to achieve high reward without achieving the
intended goal, loop agents exploit verification gaps:
• Test deletion: The simplest reward hack—delete the failing test to make CI green.
• Metric gaming: Overfitting to validation loss by memorizing the validation set rather than
generalizing.
• Specification narrowing: Solving an easier version of the stated problem that happens to
pass the checks.
• Output masking: Suppressing error output rather than fixing the underlying cause.
The defense is the same as in RLHF: design reward functions (verification criteria) that are
hard to game. Multiple independent checks—tests and type checking and linting and a review
sub-agent—create a verification surface that is much harder to exploit than any single signal.

19.9.4

Context Degradation

In long-running loops, the context window fills with the history of every step—thoughts, tool outputs,
errors, patches. As the window approaches capacity, the model’s attention to relevant information
degrades (the “lost in the middle” phenomenon [238]). Symptoms include:
• The agent re-attempts approaches it has already tried and explicitly noted as failures
• Tool calls become less precise—the agent forgets which files it has already read
• Responses become shorter and less coherent as the model struggles to attend across a bloated
context
Countermeasures:
1. Aggressive compaction: After every k steps, summarize completed work into a brief state
description and discard raw transcripts.
2. External scratchpad: Write intermediate results to files that the agent reads on-demand
rather than keeping everything in context.
3. Sub-agent isolation: Spawn subtasks in fresh context windows that return only their
conclusion—not their full reasoning trace.
4. Sliding window over history: Keep only the last w steps in full detail; compress everything
earlier into a summary block.

19.10

Production Loop Architectures

19.10.1

The Nightly Maintenance Loop

The most immediately practical loop pattern: a scheduled automation that runs overnight, processing
accumulated work while the team sleeps.
Architecture: Nightly CI Triage and Fix Loop
Trigger: Cron schedule (e.g., 02:00 UTC daily).
Phase 1 — Triage (single agent, read-only):
• Read yesterday’s CI failures, newly opened issues, and recent commits
428

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

• Classify each finding: auto-fixable / needs-human / false-positive
• Write findings to a state file; archive false positives
Phase 2 — Fix (parallel sub-agents, isolated worktrees):
• For each auto-fixable issue, spawn a sub-agent in an isolated worktree
• Each sub-agent runs a validation loop (fix → test → retry)
• Budget: 20 steps or 15 minutes per issue
Phase 3 — Review (separate verification agent):
• A review sub-agent evaluates each proposed fix against project coding standards
• Approved fixes: open draft PR, link to issue, notify channel via connector
• Rejected fixes: log rejection reason, escalate to human triage inbox
Persistence: State file (committed to repo) records all actions taken, enabling the next night’s
run to skip resolved issues and pick up where failures left off.

19.10.2

The Continuous Experimentation Loop

Inspired by AutoResearch [189], this pattern applies the loop to scientific discovery: modify a training
script, run a time-bounded experiment, evaluate the result, and decide whether to commit or rollback.
AutoResearch Loop Structure
1. Hypothesis generation: Agent proposes a modification (hyperparameter, architecture
change, data augmentation)
2. Implementation: Agent modifies the training script
3. Bounded execution: Run for exactly T minutes (hard wall-clock cap)
4. Evaluation: Read validation metric from output
5. Decision: If metric improved → git commit; if degraded → git rollback
6. Log: Record hypothesis, result, and reasoning in experiment log
7. Repeat: Generate next hypothesis informed by cumulative experiment history
Key constraint: The bounded execution time prevents any single failed experiment from
consuming excessive compute. The git-based commit/rollback ensures the codebase only moves
forward.
The Local Minimum Problem in Research Loops
Research loops are susceptible to conservative exploration. When facing difficult optimization
landscapes, agents tend to propose minimal changes—adjusting a learning rate by 0.001—that
produce nominal improvements without genuine progress. This is the RL exploration problem
manifesting at the loop level. Countermeasures include periodic “bold hypothesis” prompts,
diversity bonuses for trying novel approaches, and human-injected research directions between
runs.

19.10.3

The Always-On Orchestrator

Systems like OpenClaw [357] implement a persistent “heartbeat” mechanism: a meta-agent that runs
on a fixed cycle, evaluates repository state, supervises sub-loops, and dispatches work. Unlike the
429

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

nightly pattern which fires once per day, the always-on orchestrator maintains continuous awareness
and responds to events (new commits, failing CI, incoming issues) within minutes.
The architecture introduces a durable state database with crash recovery—if the orchestrator fails
mid-cycle, it resumes from its last checkpointed state rather than restarting from scratch. Sub-loops
are tracked as independent tasks with their own termination conditions, and the orchestrator monitors
them for stagnation, budget exhaustion, or conflict.

19.10.4

Parallel Subagent Fleet Execution

The nightly and always-on patterns both spawn sub-agents, but treat parallelism as a secondary
concern. Fleet execution makes parallelism the primary design axis: the harness is built around
the assumption that dozens or hundreds of subagents will run simultaneously, and the engineering
challenge is managing them efficiently.
Harness execution modes.
subagent execution:

Production harnesses support three distinct modes for parallel

1. Fan-out / fan-in: The orchestrator decomposes a task into N independent subtasks, dispatches
all N simultaneously, and waits for all to complete before synthesizing results. This is the
simplest parallel pattern and works well when subtasks are truly independent. The critical
constraint is that the synthesis step must handle partial failures gracefully—if 2 of 10 subtasks
fail, the orchestrator should synthesize from the 8 successes rather than failing entirely.
2. Speculative execution: The orchestrator dispatches multiple agents to attempt the same
task with different strategies (different prompts, different tool sequences, different models), then
selects the best result. This trades compute for reliability: the probability that all agents fail
is the product of individual failure probabilities. For high-stakes tasks where a single agent’s
failure rate is 20%, running 3 speculative agents reduces the failure rate to 0.23 = 0.8%.
3. Pipeline parallelism: Subtasks form a dependency graph; the harness executes all tasks
whose dependencies are satisfied simultaneously. As each task completes, it unlocks downstream
tasks. This is the most general pattern and subsumes fan-out/fan-in as a special case (a
two-level dependency graph). LangGraph’s conditional edges and parallel branches implement
this pattern natively.
Table 19.3: Parallel subagent execution modes.

Mode

When to use

Key challenge

Isolation requirements. Parallel subagents must be isolated from each other to prevent write
conflicts and context contamination. The standard approach is git worktrees for file-system isolation
(each agent operates on its own branch) combined with separate context windows (no shared
memory between agents). Shared state, when needed, should be mediated through a structured
blackboard (Section 26.3.1) with explicit locking, not through direct file sharing.
Budget management. Fleet execution can consume tokens and compute rapidly. Each subagent
should have an individual budget cap (maximum steps, maximum tokens, maximum wall-clock time),
and the orchestrator should have a fleet-level budget that it distributes across agents. When the
fleet budget is exhausted, the orchestrator should terminate remaining agents and synthesize from
completed results rather than waiting indefinitely.
430

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

Fleet Execution Checklist
1. Define subtask independence: can subtasks run in parallel without write conflicts?
2. Set per-agent budgets: steps, tokens, wall-clock time.
3. Set fleet-level budget: total cost cap across all agents.
4. Implement partial-success synthesis: handle k-of-N completions gracefully.
5. Use worktrees or containers for file-system isolation.
6. Attach correlation IDs to all agent traces for post-hoc debugging.

19.11

Context Management in Long-Running Loops

Long-running loops face a fundamental tension: the context window is the agent’s working memory,
but it has a fixed capacity. Every step appends new information (thoughts, observations, errors),
and without active management the window fills and quality degrades. This section presents the
engineering techniques for maintaining context health across many iterations.

19.11.1

The optimal strategy depends on the task. For debugging loops, a sliding window works well—

19.11.2

The Context Budget

A practical heuristic: reserve 20–30% of the context window for the current step’s reasoning and
generation. This means active history should not exceed 70–80% of capacity. When this threshold is
approached, trigger compaction before the next iteration—not after the model has already produced
degraded output.

19.12

When Not to Use Loops

Loop engineering is not universally applicable. It adds complexity, cost, and failure modes that are
unjustified when simpler approaches suffice. Prefer direct prompting or simple workflows when:
• The task is single-turn: A well-crafted prompt produces the correct answer in one shot most
of the time. Adding a loop provides marginal quality improvement at significant cost.
• The goal lacks a checkable condition: “Make the code better” has no objective stopping
point. The loop will either run forever or stop arbitrarily.
• Human interaction is cheap: If a developer is actively working and can provide feedback in
real-time, the interactive chat modality is faster than engineering a loop.
• The task exceeds model capability: If the agent cannot solve the problem in principle—
regardless of iteration count—a loop merely burns tokens. No amount of retry fixes a fundamental capability gap.
• Verification is impossible: Without a feedback signal, the loop has no gradient. It degenerates
into random search.
The Simplicity Principle
The same design principle articulated in Chapter 21 applies: start with the simplest approach that
works, and add loop complexity only when you have evidence that iteration materially improves
outcomes. A prompt chain that solves the problem is always preferable to a loop that might.

19.13

The Economics of Loops

Loops trade compute (tokens, wall-clock time) for quality. Understanding this trade-off is essential
for production deployment.
Loop Cost Model
For a loop with average N iterations, each consuming T tokens at price p per token:
Costloop = N · T · p + Costtools + Costverification
With prompt caching (where the system prompt and early context are cached and charged at
reduced rate pc < p):
Costcached = Tnew · p + Tcached · pc + (tools + verification)
Prompt caching is particularly valuable for loops because the goal specification, skill content, and
early history remain constant across iterations—often 60–80% of each call’s context is cacheable.
The economic decision: is the value of the loop’s output (developer time saved, overnight productivity, quality improvement) greater than its token cost? For a loop that runs 20 iterations at
$0.02/iteration, the total cost is $0.40—trivial if it saves 30 minutes of developer time. But a runaway
loop without budget caps can consume hundreds of dollars in a single night.

19.14

Historical Context and Related Work

Loop engineering did not emerge from a vacuum. It productized a research lineage spanning several
years:
1. ReAct (2022) [430]: Established the interleaved reasoning-and-action pattern that all modern
loops inherit.
432

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

2. Reflexion (2023) [344]: Added episodic memory and self-critique, demonstrating that agents
can improve across attempts without weight updates.
3. AutoGPT (2023) [348]: The first widely-used autonomous agent loop, demonstrating both
the potential and the pitfalls (runaway execution, high cost, unreliable output) of unattended
operation.
4. Self-Refine (2023) [259]: Formalized the generate-then-critique loop with iterative refinement.
5. “Ralph loops” (2025): Informal bash-based one-liner scripts that ran coding agents in simple
retry loops—the precursor to productized loop primitives.
6. Productized loops (2026): Major platforms (Codex, Claude Code) embedded /goal and
/loop commands directly, making sophisticated loop patterns accessible without custom
infrastructure [295].
The progression from AutoGPT to modern loop engineering illustrates a maturation: early systems
lacked termination logic, verification, and cost controls—they were loops without engineering. The
2026 formalization added the discipline that makes unattended operation safe: explicit termination,
deterministic verification, budget constraints, and maker–checker separation.

19.15

Summary

Loop engineering represents the current frontier of human–agent collaboration: the shift from
participating in conversations to designing systems that have those conversations autonomously. Its
key principles:
1. A loop is inference-time RL—state, action, reward, and policy update (via context)—operating
without gradient descent.
2. Verification is the reward signal. Its quality determines convergence. Prefer deterministic
checks; separate the maker from the checker.
3. Termination is half the design. Every loop needs a hard cap, a budget, and no-progress
detection.
4. Context is finite working memory. Manage it actively through compaction, externalization,
and sub-agent isolation.
5. Loops amplify engineering skill—they do not replace it. A loop with a poorly specified objective
will pursue the wrong thing efficiently.
6. Start simple. A single validation loop with a deterministic verifier outperforms an elaborate
multi-agent system you cannot debug.
Build the Loop—Stay the Engineer
The leverage point has moved from writing prompts to designing cycles. But designing a cycle
that converges requires understanding the problem deeply enough to specify what “done” means,
what constitutes progress, and when to stop. Loop engineering makes the human’s judgment more
important, not less—because the consequences of bad judgment now compound at machine speed.

433

Chapter 20

Graph Engineering
Loops are sufficient for homogeneous tasks. Real-world agentic workflows are heterogeneous: different
subtasks require different models, different tools, different retry budgets, and different verification
strategies. Forcing this heterogeneity into a single loop produces brittle, monolithic code. A
graph makes the structure explicit — nodes are single-responsibility units of work, edges are typed
transitions, and the topology is a first-class design artifact that can be read, tested, and reasoned
about independently of the code inside each node. This chapter covers graph engineering as the
topology layer of agentic system design, with a full LangGraph reference implementation.
GAS Connection — Graph Engineering
The GAS Supervisor is a LangGraph state machine—a directed graph of agent invocations. The
following chapter’s treatment of graph primitives, topologies, state management, and LangGraph implementation is the direct specification for build_gas_graph() in capstone_gas/gas_system.py.
Graph primitives (§ Graph Primitives). The GAS graph has five node types registered
via builder.add_node(): "monitor" (monitor_node), "advisor" (advisor_node), "safety"
(safety_node), "caregiver" (caregiver_node), and "supervisor" (supervisor_node).
Edges are conditional: the transition from "supervisor" to "advisor" fires only if
state["next_agent"] == "advisor".
Core graph topology (§ Core Graph Topologies). The GAS graph is a sequential with
conditional branching topology. The main path is START → monitor → supervisor → advisor
→ supervisor → safety → supervisor → caregiver → END. Conditional branches allow
skipping the Advisor (if alert level is low) or retrying the Advisor (if Safety Critic rejects the
recommendation).
State management (§ State Management in Graphs). The LangGraph state object is the
GASState TypedDict with fields: patient, readings_history, current_reading, alert_level,
alert_reason, recommendation, safety_score, safety_approved, caregiver_notified,
agent_messages, next_agent, iteration. Each agent node reads from and writes to this shared
state. LangGraph’s immutable state updates make the pipeline auditable: the full state history is
preserved by the MemorySaver checkpointer.
LangGraph implementation (§ Graph Engineering with LangGraph).
The
GAS graph is defined using LangGraph’s StateGraph API: nodes are registered with
builder.add_node(), fixed edges with builder.add_edge(), and conditional edges with
builder.add_conditional_edges(). The compiled graph is returned by build_gas_graph()
and is callable: it takes a GASState and returns a final GASState.
Failure modes (§ Failure Modes and Anti-Patterns). The GAS graph has one known
failure mode: if the Safety Critic rejects a recommendation and the Advisor generates a new one,
the graph can cycle between advisor and safety indefinitely. This is prevented by the iteration
counter in GASState: after 2 Advisor–Safety Critic cycles, the Supervisor routes to END and flags
the case for human review.
If loop engineering is the discipline of designing iterative control structures that drive an agent
toward a goal, then graph engineering is the discipline of designing the topology of those structures—
specifying not just that an agent loops, but which nodes execute, in what order, under what conditions,
434

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

and with what shared state. Where a loop is a single cycle, a graph is a network of cycles, branches,
and parallel paths that can express arbitrarily complex agent workflows.
The emergence of graph engineering as a distinct discipline reflects a maturation in how practitioners
think about agentic systems. Early agents were linear: prompt → response. Loop engineering
added iteration. Graph engineering adds structure: the ability to route control flow conditionally,
execute subtasks in parallel, compose reusable subgraphs, and maintain typed shared state across a
heterogeneous network of agent nodes.
The Engineering Progression: Graphs as the Next Layer
1. Prompt engineering: Optimize what you say to the model (2022–2024)
2. Context engineering: Optimize everything the model sees (2025)
3. Harness engineering: Optimize the environment the agent runs in (2025–2026)
4. Loop engineering: Optimize the cycle that keeps the agent working toward a goal (2026)
5. Graph engineering: Optimize the topology of the entire agent workflow (2026–)
Each layer wraps the previous one. A graph is a generalization of a loop: every loop is a graph
with a single cycle. Graph engineering adds the tools to reason about, compose, and debug the
full structure of a multi-step, multi-agent system.

20.1

Why Graphs? From Loops to Topologies

A loop is sufficient when a task has a single, homogeneous retry structure: generate, verify, retry. But
most real-world agentic tasks are heterogeneous: different subtasks require different tools, different
models, different verification strategies, and different retry budgets. Forcing this heterogeneity into a
single loop produces brittle, monolithic code. A graph makes the structure explicit.
Consider a document-processing pipeline: a document must be (1) classified, then (2a) summarized
if it is a report or (2b) extracted for entities if it is a contract, then (3) both outputs are merged,
and finally (4) the result is validated. This workflow has a branch, a parallel execution, a merge, and
a verification step. Expressing it as a loop requires ad-hoc conditionals scattered through the loop
body. Expressing it as a graph makes the topology visible, testable, and reusable.
Loops vs. Graphs: The Core Distinction
A loop asks: “How many times should I retry this step?”
A graph asks: “Which step should execute next, given the current state?”
Loops are about iteration. Graphs are about routing. In practice, most production agentic systems
are graphs that contain loops as substructures—cycles in the graph that implement retry logic for
individual nodes.

20.2

Graph Primitives

A computational graph for agentic AI is formally a directed graph G = (N , E, S) where:
• N is a set of nodes, each representing a unit of computation (an LLM call, a tool invocation,
a human checkpoint, or a subgraph).
• E ⊆ N × N is a set of edges, each representing a possible transition between nodes.
• S is a shared state schema, a typed data structure that all nodes read from and write to.
Unlike a pure DAG (directed acyclic graph), agentic graphs may contain cycles—edges that route
control back to an earlier node to implement retry or refinement loops. The graph is therefore a
directed graph with optional cycles, sometimes called a cyclic computation graph or a stateful
workflow graph.
435

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

A node is a function fi : S → S that reads from the shared state, performs some computation, and
writes its output back to the state. Nodes are the atomic units of work in a graph. Common node
types:

Edges and Routing

Edges define the possible transitions between nodes. There are two kinds:
• Unconditional edges: Always traverse to the target node after the source completes. Used
for sequential steps with no branching.
• Conditional edges: A routing function r : S → N inspects the current state and returns the
next node to execute. This is the mechanism for branching, looping, and dynamic dispatch.
Conditional edges are the most powerful primitive in graph engineering. They allow the graph to
adapt its execution path based on intermediate results—routing to a retry node if verification fails,
to a human checkpoint if confidence is low, or to a specialized subgraph if the input belongs to a
particular category.
Conditional Edge: Route by Document Type

20.2.3

Shared State

The shared state S is the graph’s working memory—a typed data structure that persists across all
node executions within a single graph run. Every node reads from and writes to this state; the graph
runtime manages its lifecycle.
State design is one of the most consequential decisions in graph engineering. A well-designed state
schema:
• Is typed: Each field has a declared type, enabling static validation and IDE support.
• Is append-only for lists: Rather than overwriting message history, nodes append to it—
preserving the full trace for debugging and context management.
• Is minimal: Contains only what nodes need to communicate. Bloated state schemas create
implicit coupling between nodes.
• Is serializable: Can be checkpointed to disk, enabling pause-and-resume and crash recovery.
Typed State Schema (LangGraph-style)
from typing import TypedDict , Annotated , List
import operator
class GraphState ( TypedDict ) :
# Input
document : str
# Classification output
doc_type : str
confidence : float
# Processing outputs ( append - only via operator . add )
messages : Annotated [ List [ str ] , operator . add ]
# Verification
verified : bool
retry_count : int
# Final output
result : str

The Annotated[List[str], operator.add] pattern tells the graph runtime to merge (append)
updates to messages rather than overwrite them—a critical design choice for preserving history
across parallel branches.

20.3

Core Graph Topologies

Six fundamental topologies cover the vast majority of agentic graph patterns. More complex graphs
are compositions of these primitives.

20.3.1

Linear Chain

The simplest topology: nodes execute sequentially, each passing its output to the next. Equivalent to
a prompt chain or a pipeline. Use when the task has a fixed sequence of steps with no branching or
retry.
N1 → N2 → N3 → · · · → Nk
When to use: Document transformation pipelines, multi-step reasoning with fixed structure,
preprocessing chains.
Limitation: No adaptability. If any node fails, the entire chain fails with no recovery path.
437

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

20.3.2

Branch and Merge (Fan-Out / Fan-In)

A router node dispatches to one of several specialized branches; a merge node aggregates their
outputs. The branches may execute sequentially (one chosen path) or in parallel (all paths, results
merged).
Branch A

Router

Merge

Branch B

Branch C

When to use: Tasks with mutually exclusive subtypes (route to specialist), or tasks that benefit
from parallel execution (run multiple retrievers simultaneously, merge results).
Key design choice: Is the fan-out exclusive (one branch executes) or parallel (all branches
execute)? Exclusive fan-out uses a conditional edge; parallel fan-out uses a Send primitive or
equivalent that spawns concurrent executions.

20.3.3

Cycle (Retry Loop)

A back-edge from a later node to an earlier one implements a retry loop within the graph. The cycle
continues until a termination condition is met—identical in structure to the validation loop from
Chapter 19, but expressed as a graph topology rather than an imperative for loop.
fail

Ngenerate → Nverify −−→ Ngenerate
pass

Nverify −−→ Noutput

(cycle)

(exit)

When to use: Any step that requires iterative refinement—code generation, structured output
extraction, plan revision.
Critical requirement: Every cycle must have a termination guard—a condition that exits the
cycle after a maximum number of iterations or when a budget is exhausted. A cycle without a
termination guard is an infinite loop.
Cycles Require Explicit Termination Guards
Unlike a for loop in code, a graph cycle has no implicit iteration count. The routing function
that creates the back-edge must also check a retry_count field in the state and route to an error
or escalation node when the limit is reached. Omitting this guard is the most common cause of
runaway graph execution.

20.3.4

Hierarchical Subgraph

A node in the parent graph encapsulates an entire child graph. The child graph receives a subset
of the parent state, executes to completion, and returns its output to the parent state. This is the
graph-engineering equivalent of a function call—it enables modularity, reuse, and independent testing
of subcomponents.
Subgraph Composition
# Define a reusable " research " subgraph
research_graph = StateGraph ( ResearchState )
research_graph . add_node ( " search " , web_search_node )
research_graph . add_node ( " synthesize " , synthesis_node )
research_graph . add_edge ( " search " , " synthesize " )
rese arch_ subgraph = research_graph . compile ()
# Embed it as a node in the parent graph
parent_graph = StateGraph ( ParentState )

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

parent_graph . add_node ( " plan " , planning_node )
parent_graph . add_node ( " research " , research_subgraph )
parent_graph . add_node ( " write " , writing_node )
parent_graph . add_edge ( " plan " , " research " )
parent_graph . add_edge ( " research " , " write " )

# subgraph as node

When to use: Reusable workflows (a “research” subgraph used by multiple parent graphs),
complex subtasks that warrant independent testing, and multi-agent systems where each agent is a
subgraph.

20.3.5

Map-Reduce

A map node dynamically generates a list of work items and dispatches each to a worker subgraph in
parallel; a reduce node aggregates the results. Unlike static fan-out (where the number of branches is
fixed at graph-definition time), map-reduce handles dynamic parallelism—the number of parallel
workers is determined at runtime by the data.
Map-Reduce in Agentic Graphs
Map phase: Given a list of k items (documents, subtasks, hypotheses), spawn k parallel worker
executions, each processing one item.
Reduce phase: Collect all k results and aggregate them (summarize, vote, merge, rank).
Example: A research agent that generates 5 search queries, executes all 5 in parallel, and
synthesizes the results into a single answer. The number of queries (5) is determined at runtime,
not at graph-definition time.
Implementation: Frameworks like LangGraph [164] implement this via a Send API that dynamically creates parallel graph invocations from a list.

20.3.6

Supervisor–Worker

A supervisor node maintains a task queue and dispatches items to worker nodes. Workers report results
back to the supervisor, which decides whether to dispatch more work, retry failed items, or terminate.
This topology implements the maker–checker separation from loop engineering (Section 19.3.1) at
the graph level.

Figure 20.1: Supervisor–worker topology. The supervisor node routes tasks to specialized workers and
aggregates their outputs. Each worker may itself contain a retry cycle.

20.4

State Management in Graphs

State management is the central engineering challenge of graph design. Unlike a loop—where state
is a single evolving context window—a graph may have multiple concurrent execution paths, each
modifying state simultaneously. This introduces concurrency, consistency, and persistence challenges
that do not arise in sequential loops.
439

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

20.4.1

State Update Semantics

When two parallel branches both write to the same state field, the graph runtime must decide how
to merge their updates. There are three common semantics:
Table 20.2: State update semantics for concurrent graph branches.

Semantic

Behavior

Use Case

Last-write-wins

The last branch to complete overwrites the field
Each branch appends to a
list; all writes are preserved
A custom function combines all branch outputs

Scalar outputs where only one
branch is authoritative
Message history, retrieved documents, candidate answers
Voting, averaging scores, deduplicating results

Append
Merge function

The choice of update semantic must be declared in the state schema (as in the Annotated example
above) and must match the graph’s topology. Using last-write-wins for a field that two parallel
branches both write to produces non-deterministic behavior—a common source of subtle bugs in
parallel graph execution.

20.4.2

Checkpointing and Persistence

A graph run may span many seconds or minutes. Checkpointing—persisting the full graph state
after each node execution—enables:
1. Crash recovery: If the process dies mid-execution, the graph resumes from the last checkpoint
rather than restarting from scratch.
2. Human-in-the-loop: The graph pauses at a human node, persists state, and waits for
input—potentially for hours or days—before resuming.
3. Time travel: Inspecting or replaying the graph from any prior checkpoint, enabling debugging
and counterfactual analysis.
4. Branching: Creating multiple execution branches from the same checkpoint to explore
alternative paths (analogous to Monte Carlo Tree Search at the graph level).
Checkpointing as the Graph’s External State
In loop engineering (Section 19.3.2), external state connects iterations across time. In graph
engineering, checkpointing plays the same role—but with richer semantics. A checkpoint captures
not just the current state values but the full execution history: which nodes have run, in what
order, with what inputs and outputs. This makes graph checkpoints far more useful for debugging
than a simple state file.

20.4.3

Thread Isolation

Production graph systems support multiple concurrent graph runs, each identified by a thread ID.
Each thread has its own isolated state and checkpoint history. Thread isolation enables:
• Multi-user systems: Each user’s conversation or task runs in its own thread, with no state
leakage between users.
• Parallel experimentation: Multiple graph configurations run simultaneously on the same
input, with results compared across threads.
• Long-running tasks: A thread can be paused, resumed, and inspected independently of other
threads.
440

H. Roitman — The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems

20.5

Graph Engineering vs. Loop Engineering

Graph engineering and loop engineering are complementary, not competing. Understanding when to
use each—and how to combine them—is a core skill.

When to Use a Loop vs. a Graph
Use a loop when:
• The task has a single, homogeneous retry structure (generate → verify → retry)
• The workflow is simple enough to fit in a single function
• You need minimal infrastructure overhead
Use a graph when:
• The workflow has multiple distinct steps with different tools, models, or verification strategies
• You need conditional branching based on intermediate results
• You need parallel execution of independent subtasks
• You need human-in-the-loop checkpoints
• You need to compose reusable subgraphs across multiple workflows
• You need crash recovery and time-travel debugging
In practice: start with a loop. When the loop body accumulates more than 3–4 distinct phases
with different logic, refactor to a graph.

20.6.3

The Human-in-the-Loop Graph

For high-stakes workflows, the graph pauses at designated human nodes, persists state, and waits for
approval before proceeding. This is the graph-engineering implementation of the human-in-the-loop
pattern discussed in Chapter 21.
Human-in-the-Loop via Graph Interrupts
LangGraph [164] implements human-in-the-loop via interrupt points: nodes designated as
requiring human approval before the graph continues. When the graph reaches an interrupt node:
1. The current state is checkpointed to persistent storage.
2. The graph execution pauses and returns control to the caller.
3. A human reviews the state (e.g., via a UI or API call) and provides input.
4. The graph resumes from the checkpoint with the human’s input injected into the state.
This pattern enables workflows that span hours or days—the graph is not running continuously,
but its state is preserved across the pause. The human’s review is just another node in the graph,
with the same state-read/state-write interface as any other node.

points—in a Python API that integrates with the LangChain ecosystem. Chapter 27.3.1 provides a
detailed walkthrough of LangGraph’s architecture and code patterns; this section focuses on how its
API maps to the graph engineering primitives introduced above.
Other notable frameworks include AutoGen [407] (Microsoft’s multi-agent conversation graph
framework), CrewAI [275] (role-based agent orchestration), and general-purpose workflow engines
such as Prefect and Temporal that can host agentic graphs as durable tasks. The choice of framework
